US card checkout / return detection playbook

If the card tester returns
recognize the pattern and respond sooner

Watch how cards are tested across accounts and processors. Use the old profile as supporting evidence, even when the next wave arrives with different names, phones or browsers.

9 November 2026   |   Based on the 22 September to 31 October attack   |   Current production settings not independently checked

These details can change quickly

Useful clues, but insufficient on their own.

  • Email pattern and domain
  • Phone number, changed in about 5 hours
  • Billing address and postcode
  • Browser string and claimed app version
  • Internet address, rotated across identities

Keep the known indicators, but do not wait for an exact match. A new disguise must not be the only reason an alert stays quiet.

Watch for these behaviors together

Historical clues to suspected card testing, not proof of the same person or group.

A burst of new accounts1,086 sign-ups in one hour after the account throttle began.
Declines spread across accountsThe attacker reduced tries per account and moved to fresh accounts.
Many different cardsRepeated card changes with few approvals. Watch across accounts, not just within one.
Shared card rangesRuns on the same card prefix supported the earlier pattern. A prefix alone is not a reason to block.
Missing or failed bot checksMonitor reCAPTCHA failures at sign-up and checkout, including blocked requests.
Repeated automated timingMedian 10 seconds between tries in the workbook. Slower attempts can still be an attack.

No fixed checklist proves identity. Correlate signals and validate the linked activity. These behaviors can change too.

When an alert fires, act across the whole payment path

Proposed response targets and roles, not measured performance
Within 5 minutes of a qualifying pattern

1   Confirm and page

Validate connected accounts, cards and declines. Check Worldpay, Nuvei and Global Payments together. Notify the incident owner.

Payment Operations + on-call owner
Within 15 minutes of a qualifying pattern

2   Contain the attempts

Challenge or temporarily restrict affected traffic. Apply the fraud decision before the first processor call and any backup retry.

DevOps + application owners
After containment

3   Check the outcome

Review suspicious approvals for void or refund. Check for attempts on another route and legitimate customers affected by the controls.

Payments + incident owner

Protect real customers: no postcode-only bans, blanket card-range bans, or gateway internet-address limits that group real customers together. Confirm normal traffic and a recovery path before enforcing new limits.

Before relying on this plan
Name one incident owner and backup. Verify settings, calibrate thresholds, and test that alerts reach the on-call team.

Measure whether we improved
Time from first suspicious activity to alert and containment; attempts reaching processors after the alert; legitimate customers challenged or blocked.

These files are historical evidence, not a live configuration audit. The earlier attack's identity and location remain unestablished. No guarantee is made that a future attack will repeat any particular signal. The 80% in the alarm row is a proposed/reported rule threshold, not a measured success rate. The earlier card-limit effectiveness figures were simulations and are intentionally not presented as live protection.
